newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African bond yields seen retracing post-budget.
newsitem.headline: S.African bond yields seen retracing post-budget.

text.p: South Africa's bond market is expected to focus on the continuing liquidity squeeze on the money market now that the 1997/98 budget has been announced, analysts said on Thursday.

Despite the generally positive perceptions of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's budget, bond traders said on Thursday most of the bullish news that had come out of the budget had been priced into the market and players were now turning their attention to more immediate concerns.
Societe Generale Frankel Pollak gilts analyst Tertia Jacobs said that in the next quarter bond market yields were likely to move higher.
"As far as we are concerned most of the news in the budget has been discounted and the market is running on sentiment now," she said.

"In the short term we could be in for a bit of a correction as people start looking at other fundamentals like the money market, the fact that inflation still has not peaked and that economic growth might be doing better than we first thought it was," Jacobs said.

Short-term deposit rates, which have hovered around the 16.50 percent offered rate in recent weeks, have been hamstrung by the money market shortage's inability to sustain a move below the 10 billion rand mark since the beginning of the year.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has said the central bank is keen to keep the shortage at a high level to assist it in its efforts to rein in profligate consumer credit spending.

Jacobs added, however, that she expected the bond market to firm again in the medium term, particularly as the fundamentals could warrant lower interest rates and lower inflation later in the year, which could support institutional and foreign investment in the market.

The South African bond market's status as flavour of the month is borne out by Bond Exchange figures which show foreigners have been net buyers of local gilts to the tune of 1.08 billion rand in the last two days alone.
That brings total purchases so far this year to 3.75 billion rand -- 11 percent more than they bought during the whole of 1996.

Annelise Peers, fixed interest analyst at Investec Securities, said while foreign investors were aware of pressures on the money market as well as the spectre of rising inflation, their more immediate concern was the budget.

"Foreigners are taking a big picture view of it. Yes, the numbers are not looking great at the moment but the general expectation is that they will improve towards the latter half of this year," she said.
"The foreigners waited for the budget to get out of the way because South Africa is definitely on their list to buy this year," Peers said.
She said the only concern among foreign investors was the recent uncertainty on the U.S. bond market, where yields have risen amid fears of a hike in interest rates.

"South African bond market yields provide very good returns relative to other emerging markets and other markets. The only thing that upset it a little bit was uncertainty on the U.S. market, which is still hanging around," Peers said.
She said if yields did move higher, they were likely to be capped at the 15 percent level.

"It is difficult to say whether we can go lower from current levels...if the U.S. market stabilises, when people move back to emerging markets South Africa will be the first market they move into," she said.
